Isodar-adjusted inequality (IAI)

Source: R/iai.R
iai.Rd

Computes niche breadth from fitted isodars by allocating a given total abundance among habitats according to the isodars and measuring the inequality of that allocation (1 - Gini). Evaluating it at several totals gives a rarefaction-like curve of niche breadth against abundance.

Usage

iai(
  isodars,
  abundances = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  scaled = TRUE,
  min_occupancy = 1,
  max_search = 10000,
  dim = NULL,
  plot = FALSE,
  method = "gini"
)

Arguments

isodars

Output of fit_isodars().

abundances

Numeric vector of total abundances, or NULL for the density-independent value.

weights

Pairwise only: NULL (equal weights), "1/var" (inverse variance of each isodar's vertical residuals, \(1/(sd^2(1+b^2))\)), or a numeric vector with one weight per isodar.

scaled

If TRUE, 1 - Gini is rescaled to 0-1, so that a species found in a single habitat scores 0 and an even spread scores 1.

min_occupancy

Individuals required in every habitat for the density-independent value.

max_search

Largest total searched for the density-independent value.

dim

Optional; inferred from isodars. Kept for compatibility.

plot

If TRUE and several abundances are given, plots the curve.

method

Inequality measure; only "gini" is currently implemented.

Value

A tibble with total_abundance, niche_breadth, one column per habitat (predicted abundance), and note.

Details

Allocation. For pairwise isodars, the predicted abundances are those that minimise the (optionally weighted) sum of squared deviations from all pairwise isodar equations, \(y - b x = a\), subject to summing to the total. This constrained least-squares problem is solved directly; habitats predicted to be negative are set to zero and the rest are solved again. For an n-dimensional isodar (a line), the allocation is the single point at which the line reaches the total; negative habitats are set to zero.

Density-independent niche breadth (abundances = NULL) is evaluated at the smallest total (searched over integers) at which every used habitat holds at least min_occupancy individuals. If no total up to max_search achieves this, a single row with NA is returned.

Absent habitats (see fit_isodars()) are fixed at 0 and count as 0 in the inequality, so they lower niche breadth; with a single used habitat, niche breadth is 0.

Density-dependent niche breadth is the value at a high total abundance, supplied through abundances.

See also

fit_isodars(), isoderr(), pairwise_niche()

Examples

set.seed(1)
sim <- simulate_isodars(1.5, 1.5, 5, 5, noise = 1, n = 30)
pw <- fit_isodars(sim, hab_cols = c("hab1", "hab2", "hab3"))
iai(pw)                          # density-independent
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   total_abundance niche_breadth  hab1  hab2  hab3 note 
#>             <dbl>         <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr>
#> 1              23         0.381  1.03  6.70  15.3 ""   
iai(pw, abundances = c(50, 500)) # density-dependent
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   total_abundance niche_breadth   hab1  hab2  hab3 note 
#>             <dbl>         <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr>
#> 1              50         0.574   6.72  15.2  28.0 ""   
#> 2             500         0.721 102.   157.  241.  ""   
ln <- fit_isodars(sim, hab_cols = c("hab1", "hab2", "hab3"), dim = "ndim")
iai(ln, abundances = 500)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   total_abundance niche_breadth  hab1  hab2  hab3 note 
#>             <dbl>         <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr>
#> 1             500         0.721  102.  157.  241. ""
